title: MB7-01788
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX, the principal appellant, and his two minor daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, Haitian citizens, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD).
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX, the principal appellant, and his two minor daughters, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, Haitian citizens, are appealing against the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD). They are presenting evidence in their appeal and asking that a hearing be held. They are submitting that the RPD erred by not considering the principal claimant's vulnerability and the fact that, overall, his testimony was consistent.
The principal appellant was designated as the representative of his daughters.
Under section 111 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal. I. BACKGROUND A. Summary of alleged facts

In his Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form), the principal appellant states that as an employee of the XXXX XXXX, he participated in XXXX XXXX concerning a bank robbery by a gang of criminals that occurred on XXXX XXXX, 2014. He also states that after the arrest, the trials and then the release of that gang's leader, he received several threats on his cellular telephone on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, he was the victim of attempted murder on XXXX XXXX, 2016, and his wife was killed on XXXX XXXX, 2016.

In his BOC Form, the principal appellant states that he took legal action, but it did not go anywhere. He also states that the criminals who killed his wife are actively looking for him to do the same thing to him.1 In addition to their BOC Forms, the appellants, then designated as the claimants, presented documents before the RPD.2 B. RPD decision
The hearing was held on January 17, 2017, before the RPD, and the decision to reject the refugee protection claims was rendered on February 1, 2017.

The RPD found that the principal claimant's contradictions, omissions and confusing, vague and evasive responses resulted in it not believing anything from the entire story of persecution by criminals. Therefore, it did not give any probative value to the complaint of August 18, 2016.
The RPD also found that nothing in the evidence established that the principal claimant's wife had been killed.
Finally, the RPD found that the principal claimant failed to present any evidence to establish that employees like him were particularly targeted because of their ties to the XXXX XXXX XXXX.3 II.
In their memorandum, the appellants submit that the RPD erred by failing to consider the principal claimant's vulnerability and that his testimony was generally consistent.
paragraphs.heading_before: GROUNDS OF APPEAL AND DECISION SOUGHT

paragraphs.text: In conclusion, the appellants asked the RAD to set aside the RPD's determination and grant them the status of persons in need of protection or refer the matter to the RPD for re-determination.4 III.

In their memorandum, the appellants refer to evidence that they did not present before the RPD. Except for a statement from their lawyer indicating that this evidence was presented in accordance with the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, from my perspective, in their memorandum, I did not find any full and detailed submission to establish how this evidence meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, as required by the Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules).5

In Singh, the Federal Court of Appeal held that the explicit conditions set out in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA are inescapable, have to be met and leave no room for discretion on the part of the RAD. It also held that the criteria set out in the case law with respect to the credibility and relevance of evidence arise implicitly from the wording of the subsection in question. In short, there is a clear legislative intention to not authorize any new evidence on appeal before the RAD other than in very specific and carefully defined circumstances. Its role is not to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record, but to allow errors that the RPD may have made to be corrected.6
In my opinion, the evidence presented on appeal does not meet the criteria under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Here is why.

In their memorandum, the appellants present these documents7 to establish that because the principal appellant was a victim of attempted murder on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2016, and because of his wife's murder on XXXX XXXX, 2016, he was obligated to cancel his trip and another reservation was therefore made for XXXX XXXX, 2016.

These documents simply indicate dates of departure and return on two different flights in XXXX and XXXX 2016. Therefore, they are not facts that arose after the RPD decision. The appellants failed to provide any full and detailed submission to establish how that evidence meets the requirements of the other two criteria under subsection 110(4). There is nothing to establish that it was not possible to obtain that evidence before the RPD decision was rendered or why the appellants did not present this evidence before the RPD. Therefore, I find that this evidence is not admissible on appeal.

In their memorandum, the appellants provide this prescription8 to establish that the principal appellant is on medication for stress and other conditions, adding that he requires these medications to be able to sleep because he is still affected by his wife's death.

This prescription does not include any information to establish a link between the principal appellant's health condition and his wife's death. It does not have any information about the principal appellant's health condition at the time of the hearing held before the RPD. As a result, in my opinion, this document does not concern relevant events with respect to the appellants' refugee protection claims.9 Consequently, it does not meet the criteria under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

In their memorandum, the appellants provide documents concerning the principal appellant's employment in Haiti.10 None of the information in these documents relates to facts that arose after the RPD decision. The appellants failed to provide any full and detailed submission to establish how that evidence meets the requirements of the two other criteria under subsection 110(4). There is nothing to establish that it was not possible to obtain that evidence before the RPD decision was rendered or why the appellants did not present this evidence before the RPD. Therefore, I find that this evidence is not admissible on appeal.
paragraphs.heading_before: C. Documents concerning the principal appellant's employment in Haiti

paragraphs.text: This letter was provided on April 23, 2018, after the appeal record was filed. There was no application to obtain the authorization to use it on appeal, as required by the RAD Rules.11 In addition, this document does not concern events relevant to the appellants' refugee protection claims.
paragraphs.heading_before: D. A letter regarding the principal appellant's job in 2018

paragraphs.text: In a statement from their lawyer, the appellants ask that a hearing be held before the RAD.12 Nevertheless, the onus rests with the RAD to determine whether the criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have been met.13
paragraphs.heading_before: IV. HOLDING A HEARING BEFORE THE RAD

paragraphs.text: One of the determinative criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA is that one of the pieces of evidence presented on appeal was found to be admissible. However, the documents presented by the appellants were found to be inadmissible. Consequently, there is no new documentary evidence to analyze in a hearing before the RAD.14 V. APPLICABLE STANDARD OF REVIEW AND ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

The RAD reviews RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard after conducting its own analysis of the record. The exception to this rule is, where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in assessing the credibility or weight to be given to the oral evidence it hears, the RAD must then apply the reasonableness standard modified to its particular context.15 That said, the role of the RAD is not to carry out a de novo consideration of refugee protection claims but to determine whether, as alleged by the appellants, the RPD did indeed err.16

Having conducted my own analysis of the record, including listening to the recording of the hearing held before the RPD,17 I am of the opinion that the standard of correctness must be applied, given that my own decision requires analysis of several elements with respect to which the RPD did not enjoy a meaningful advantage based on a first-hand observation of the appellant's demeanour.18 Having applied this standard of review, I find that the appellants' arguments are unfounded and that the RPD did not err in rejecting their refugee protection claims. Here is why.

Chairperson's Guideline 819 allows for procedural accommodations to be made for the particular needs of vulnerable persons. It indicates that it is preferable to identify vulnerable persons at the earliest opportunity and, in this regard, their counsel or lawyer is best placed to bring this issue to the member's attention, specifically by submitting an application under the Refugee Protection Division Rules (RPD Rules).20 During the hearing before the RPD, the issue of the principal claimant's vulnerability was never brought to the RPD's attention.
paragraphs.heading_before: A. The issue of the principal claimant's vulnerability

paragraphs.text: Even if this issue had then been addressed by the RPD and if the principal claimant had been identified as a vulnerable person, it would not have made credible a testimony that is deficient due to implausibilities or contradictions that cannot be linked to the state of vulnerability.21 B. The principal claimant's credibility was seriously undermined

In this case, having read the RPD decision, listened to the recording of the hearing before it and considered the arguments presented on appeal, I am of the opinion that the correct decision was to reject the refugee protection claims, as the omissions and contradictions in the testimony and the documentary evidence from the principal appellant were fatal to his credibility.22

First, the story presented during the hearing before the RPD, namely, that a friend of the principal claimant had been robbed by criminals while leaving a bank, was inconsistent with the one presented in the BOC Form, that is, that the principal claimant had participated in several XXXX XXXX to end criminality in his country and had been by a gang of criminals who had robbed a bank in his country. When asked to explain the difference between these two accounts, the principal claimant responded that, in his BOC Form, he simply provides a summary.23 In my opinion, I find that there was a major difference between the two accounts and that the principal claimant's explanation is unreasonable. Therefore, his credibility is seriously undermined.

Then, in his testimony about his role in the XXXX that led to the XXXX XXXX, the principal claimant was very vague. Moreover, when asked to explain why he did not submit the initial complaint regarding the robbery committed by these criminals in 2014, he simply responded that he had not thought of that.24 On this last point, it is important to point out that failing to file supporting documentation that it is reasonable to expect may have an impact on a claimant's credibility.25 In my opinion, given that the principal claimant is an employee of the XXXX XXXX XXXX who personally participated in the XXXX, it was reasonable to expect that he would file this complaint before the RPD. Again, his credibility is seriously undermined.

Finally, having found that the principal claimant generally lacked credibility, the RPD could not give any probative value to documents that merely repeated facts that it did not find to be credible.26 Moreover, the documents concerning the principal claimant's wife's death do not include any information to explain the cause.27 CONCLUSION

For these reasons, I confirm the RPD's determination, namely, that XXXX XXXX XXXX and his two minor daughters XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are not refugees under section 96 or persons in need of protection under section 97 of the IRPA.

The appeal is dismissed. Alain Bissonnette Me Alain Bissonnette November 1, 2018 Date IRB translation Original language: French 1 The principal appellant's BOC Form, pages 11 to 23 of the RPD record.
